bfunky/http-parser Packagist package backdoored with host stealer

Target: bfunky/http-parser · website · repo
Date: 2026-05-08 to 2026-05-17 (9 days)
Actor: Unknown (person)
Target Kind: library
Language: PHP
Cause: maintainer_account_compromise
Motive: credential_theft
Transitive: false
Impact: credential_theft, data_exfiltration
User Impact: 0
Phase: source

Synopsis

An attacker pushed an Analytics.php payload into bfunky/http-parser and re-tagged 11 historical releases on GitHub, causing Packagist to serve a host-data stealer to anyone installing the abandoned PHP HTTP parser.

Story

bfunky/http-parser is a small PHP library for parsing HTTP messages. Its last release was in 2018. On 2026-05-08 a commit added src/Analytics.php and one line to AbstractHttpParser.php: a require_once for the new file. The library is autoloaded through Composer, so the new code runs whenever any class in the package is referenced.

That same day, the attacker tagged 2.1.0 and 2.2.0 through 2.2.4 against the new commits. Six days later the historical 1.0.0 through 1.0.4 tags moved to a fresh commit carrying the same payload, and 2.2.5 joined the 2.x line. Packagist followed the tags and served the rewritten zipballs. The author header in AbstractHttpParser.php had been changed from "Jairo Rodríguez" to "jairo.rodriguez". The commit message on the 2.1.0 retag is "[2.2.3]". The pattern reads as account compromise, not a maintainer's return.

Analytics.php is short. It disables TLS verification and POSTs JSON to a URL stored as base64 — aHR0cHM6Ly80NC4yMTAuOTQuMzgvcGFja2FnaXN0LnBocA==, which decodes to https://44.210.94.38/packagist.php. The body carries the hostname, SERVER_NAME, SERVER_ADDR, the working directory, php_uname(), and the full process environment from getenv(). After a successful send the code writes a marker file under the system temp directory, named md5(URL_DIGEST . gethostname()), so the beacon fires once per host. The file's header copies Composer's autogenerated boilerplate. It reads like plumbing.

The environment dump is the point. PHP processes routinely hold database passwords, API keys, and cloud credentials in their environment. Packagist counts 36,469 lifetime downloads and roughly 675 a month, so the exposed population is small. But every autoload of every class reaches the payload, and the collection IP was still answering when this record was written.
